articles.title_orig: US vs China: As the world splits into AI blocs, where does Europe stand?
articles.title_zh: US vs China: As the world splits into AI blocs, where does Europe stand?
articles.content_orig:
With the two leading AI powers, the United States and China, forming their own AI blocs, other countries are manoeuvring to harness the strengths of both groupings and avoid losing out.
Europe is trying to become a third force in AI, but sovereignty is harder to achieve than simply building a home-grown model. Its prospects depend on whether it can also secure the computing power, chips and infrastructure needed to develop and run AI at scale.
As the rivalry intensifies, experts say the window for countries to be able to choose freely between the AI superpowers may be narrowing, forcing them to at one point pick between the US-led Pax Silica, which the EU is already a part of, or the China-inspired World AI Cooperation Organization. But could Europe eventually offer an alternative?
In the artificial intelligence technology race, the United States and China have formed blocs with other nations seeking to set standards and reap AI's potential benefits.
Europe and many other countries are in a dilemma: Do they go with the US’s most advanced chips and AI technologies, or join China’s more affordable, open-source AI systems?
Views in Europe have changed sharply this year as fears mount over how vulnerable the European Union is to exploitation.
Trump’s forced shutdown of Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models in June, as well as the more recent switching off of Elon Musk’s military-grade satellite network Starshield in Ukraine, have raised alarm bells in European capitals.
In June, the EU unveiled its European Technological Sovereignty Package, a wide-ranging set of proposals aimed at boosting the continent’s chip production capacity, expanding data centre capacity, supporting sustainable AI, promoting open-source software and integrating data centres into the energy grid to develop sovereign AI for energy management.
The EU has already made progress in boosting chip manufacturing capacity through its Chips Act. This includes a recent €319 million state aid package for Austrian firm Infineon Technologies to develop next-generation semiconductors, as well as €5 billion in Italy and €1.6 billion in Czechia for similar projects.
Europe also has established strengths in the semiconductor supply chain, thanks to firms such as ASML , which produces advanced lithography systems needed to manufacture chips, and Soitec , which supplies semiconductor substrates used to make them.
But the bloc’s ambitions extend beyond chipmaking. The EU is also building a federated cloud and artificial intelligence infrastructure that its architects say could fundamentally change the continent’s relationship with major US and Chinese technology providers.
Rather than building a single European cloud platform from scratch, the project connects existing national infrastructure into a federated network of nodes designed to operate across borders.
Yet Europe remains heavily dependent on foreign technology, particularly in AI. The EU has no dominant frontier AI model comparable to those developed by OpenAI , Anthropic or China’s DeepSeek , and has limited leverage over the companies building the technology. France’s Mistral is one of the few prominent European contenders.
The EU is also trying to rein in its €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China, driven in part by the bloc’s reliance on Beijing for critical raw materials and electrical components needed for AI infrastructure. Up to 90% of Europe’s rare earth elements come from China, according to Euronews reporting on the cost of reducing that dependence .
Beijing has since agreed to create a “green channel” to streamline and expedite licence approvals for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU, as part of an initial trade deal with the bloc.
Alongside efforts to build up its industrial capacity, Brussels has sought to position Europe as a global rule-setter for artificial intelligence.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen vowed that Europe would help write the rules for AI, positioning the bloc as a rule-setter on a par with Washington and Beijing. The EU’s AI Act , adopted in 2024, is billed by Brussels as the “world’s first comprehensive rules on artificial intelligence”.
The Act regulates AI according to a four-tier risk framework, with obligations increasing according to the risks posed by a system. While limited-risk applications such as spam filters face relatively light requirements, certain practices deemed to pose unacceptable risks, including social scoring, are prohibited.
But European companies, concerned that the rules could stifle innovation as they race to catch up with US and Chinese rivals, lobbied hard and secured a delay to rules covering high-risk systems through the AI Omnibus bill , amid a broader shift in the Commission’s political priorities following the 2024 EU elections.
Amid growing global calls for greater control over AI, von der Leyen said the EU’s rules put “Europe in the position to shape global efforts”.
She also said she would invite the main frontier labs “for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”. European firms have been more wary of slowing down, fearing this could be an attempt by US giants to lock in their dominance.
Kazakhstan, a Central Asian nation of about 21 million people, is a rare example of a country that has sought to bridge that gap.
Just three weeks after its AI minister Zhaslan Madiyev visited Washington in June to join the US. group working to strengthen AI supply chains, he headed to Shanghai for a signing ceremony making the Central Asian country a founding member of China’s initiative to shape the global AI agenda.
Being in Pax Silica means more technological partnerships, high-tech manufacturing jobs and a place in global AI supply chains. At the same time, as part of China’s World AI Cooperation Organization alongside 28 other initial founding countries including Pakistan and Russia, Kazakhstan hopes to also have a voice in setting regional and global AI standards.
“Everyone is hedging,” said Dana Masalimova, a former Kazakhstan diplomat and independent scholar and center associate at the Kathryn W. and Shelby Cullom Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies at Harvard University.
“We don’t want this binary choice,” she said.
Kazakhstan is benefiting from both US and Chinese investments, but is in a “very precarious spot,” Masalimova said.
It has rich critical mineral resources essential to AI development and has cheap electricity to power data centers, which have become politically fraught in the US.
Earlier this year, Kazakhstan’s government signed an investment deal worth up to $10 billion involving Nvidia to build a “data center valley” in the country.
Meanwhile, more Chinese companies are investing in Kazakhstan. Local officials say Chinese foreign direct investment in Kazakhstan reached a record $2.8 billion in 2025. Chinese leader Xi Jinping met with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in July to expand cooperation under China’s global infrastructure building Belt and Road initiative.
Both China and the US are leveraging access to AI to increase their global influence.
President Donald Trump insisted last month that “whoever wins AI, wins.” US officials and AI companies have accused China of large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American models.
Beijing has rejected those claims and says the US is pursuing an AI monopoly while restricting China’s access to some of the world’s most cutting-edge AI chips and chipmaking machinery.
Washington has signalled that Pax Silica — with China as its implicit target — is only for the trusted.
“Countries can’t be trusted partners in Pax Silica while substantively engaging in initiatives that advance a competing vision for super intelligence,” the US State Department said, using the Trump administration’s new preferred term for AI.
For its part, Beijing touts the openness and inclusiveness of its World

articles.title_orig: China slams EU’s potential new trade safeguards, says they may violate WTO rules
articles.title_zh: China slams EU’s potential new trade safeguards, says they may violate WTO rules
articles.content_orig:
Beijing vows to take ‘all necessary measures’ to defend Chinese firms as Brussels reportedly mulls imposing broader import caps
Beijing reiterated its opposition on Thursday to potential new European Union trade safeguards targeting Chinese exports, vowing to take “all necessary measures” to defend the interests of its companies.
“Artificially restricting normal trade is suspected of violating World Trade Organization rules,” said Huang Ling, spokeswoman for China’s Ministry of Commerce, at a weekly press conference.
“Far from improving the competitiveness of EU industry, it will increase the burden on downstream industries, push up inflation in the EU, and undermine the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains.”

articles.title_orig: China promotes Zhang Shengmin, key player in PLA anti-graft drive, to Politburo
articles.title_zh: China promotes Zhang Shengmin, key player in PLA anti-graft drive, to Politburo
articles.content_orig:
Official communique says 21st National Congress next year will be at China’s ‘critical stage’ on journey towards second centenary goal
Zhang, who was last year promoted to vice-chair of the Central Military Commission (CMC) top commanding body, was the military’s anti-corruption chief from 2018 until July this year, and is the top enforcer of Beijing’s fight against corruption in the People’s Liberation Army.
That drive left the seven-member body with only two men – top commander President Xi Jinping and Zhang himself. It also left both military representatives on the Politburo disgraced, leaving the decision-making body without any members from the military since January.
The promotion of Zhang, which was announced at the closing of the fifth plenum of the 20th Central Committee on Thursday, has restored a PLA general to the Politburo, although it has been the norm since 1997 to have two. It remains to be seen if Beijing intends to add another general to the Politburo at next year’s 21st Party Congress.

articles.title_orig: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines says its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing
ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia -- The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines said Thursday its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing.
The restrictions have raised concerns over potential revenue losses and disruptions to Mongolia’s massive mineral sector.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC, which operates Oyu Tolgoi, one of the world’s largest copper mines, said the number of truck convoys transporting copper concentrate across the Chinese border has fallen from the usual 12 to 13 per day to just around four. The restrictions affect vehicles crossing at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port, which is adjacent to Mongolia’s Gashuunsukhait Border Port.
The export cuts amount to a decline of about $300 million compared to normal operating conditions and could reach $1.2 billion if restrictions continue through the end of the year, local media reported on Wednesday.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC did not confirm the reported losses in a statement to The Associated Press on Thursday.
Mongolia is a major supplier of coal and copper to China, the world’s largest consumer of both commodities.
Mongolian border officials said the slowdown was related to infrastructure and technology upgrades at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port.
Authorities in China’s Inner Mongolia region did not immediately answer questions from the AP.
In August, Chinese authorities introduced an in-vehicle facial recognition system for truck drivers crossing the border, and installation and maintenance work have affected border processing capacity, according to the Mongolian border authorities.
Mongolia’s government said the Chinese embassy in Ulaanbaatar informed it that the work, originally due to end by late September according to Mongolian news reports, may continue until the end of December.
Mongolian Finance Minister Mendsaikhan Zagdjav said some ministers were instructed during a Cabinet meeting to visit the border crossing and meet with Chinese authorities, according to local news reports.
All transport routes on the Mongolian side remain open and the government was not aware of any political reasons behind the restrictions, said the minister of Road and Transport, Delgersaikhan Borkhuu.
Mongolia’s copper sector has become an increasingly important contributor to national export revenues. During the first nine months of 2026, copper concentrate exports reportedly reached 2 million tons.
The border crossing restrictions have also affected Mongolia’s coal exports through Gashuunsukhait, with the number of vehicles crossing falling to just over 1,000 a day from 1,300 a day, border authorities said.
Mongolia has abundant mineral resources, including coal, copper, gold, uranium and fluorspar, and its economy relies heavily on mining, which accounts for roughly a quarter of its GDP. It is particularly sensitive to disruptions to cross-border trade and fluctuations in commodity prices.
Last year, coal and copper concentrates together accounted for 82.3% of Mongolia’s merchandise exports, while 89.4% of total exports went to China. Mongolia was also China’s leading supplier of imported coking coal, accounting for approximately 51% of Chinese coking coal imports in 2025.

articles.title_orig: At least 13 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.title_zh: At least 13 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.content_orig:
At least 13 people have been killed after a Russian drone hit a busy platform at the main train station in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, officials said.
State rail company Ukrzaliznytsia said on Thursday that a jet-powered drone hit the platform where a train was preparing to leave for the nearby city of Zaporizhzhia.
Regional Governor, Oleksandr Hanzha, said on Telegram that at least 14 others were injured and six were in critical condition, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denounced the attack as “horrific”.
“Just how many terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on certain Russian oligarchs and the Russian energy sector, rather than de-escalating?,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
Russia also attacked Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, damaging an educational institution, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram.
Ukrainian authorities also reported overnight Russian strikes in multiple areas, including an attack in the Rivne region that killed one man.
Russian news agencies, citing the Ministry of Defence, reported that its forces struck a cargo vessel used by the Ukrainian military in the Black Sea.
Meanwhile, Russia downed most of the 613 drones launched towards Moscow overnight, in a major attack on the Russian capital, state news agency TASS reported.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that air defence forces destroyed 231 of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) on approach to the city, with the remainder neutralised on distant approaches between Wednesday evening and Thursday morning.
The Kremlin condemned the attacks on Moscow as the city hosts more than 22 African leaders at a summit, TASS reported.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was “very strange” for Kyiv to target Moscow during this time.
The Russian Defence Ministry said its air defence intercepted and destroyed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight across regions.
Debris from downed drones also caused minor damage after falling onto the territory of an unnamed industrial facility in Sterlitamak, the second-largest city in Russia’s Bashkortostan region, Mayor Emil Shaimardanov said on Telegram.
He said the plant was operating as usual and that local air defence forces had shot down all eight Ukrainian drones involved in the attack.
The attack marks the latest in a series of major drone assaults targeting the Moscow region, following a record attack in September during which air defence forces reported shooting down more than 1,600 drones.
Both sides have reported an increase in attacks in recent months, while Moscow and Kyiv also prepare to resume peace talks next month with US mediation.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian delegation has headed to the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky, where a localised ceasefire is under way to provide humanitarian aid to the remaining residents.
The Kremlin also said it hopes aid will reach Oleshky on Thursday or Friday and that those wanting to leave the town were able to do so, Russia’s Interfax news agency reported.
So far, neither Ukraine nor Russia has reported any violations of the six-day ceasefire, which took effect early Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.title_zh: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.content_orig:
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violating [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Analysts believe one reason for the increased empahsis on discipline – which many interpret as loyalty – is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."

articles.title_orig: An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
articles.title_zh: An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
articles.content_orig:
Linköping University professor Peter Jonsson is set to have his work presented in two weeks’ time at one of the most prestigious conferences in theoretical computer science. As of Monday, much of that work is “dead,” he says, after AI showed that a 27-year-old hypothesis underpinning it is wrong.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic claimed this week to have disproved the exponential time hypothesis (ETH). Vast swaths of theoretical computer science research on complexity and algorithm design have been built on the premise that the effort it takes to solve certain problems increases exponentially with the size of the problem.
Jonsson expects his predicament will be “very common” at the IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, where his work will be presented by one of his coauthors. “People will start the talks: ‘ETH is false, half of my paper does not work,’” he says. It’s a vexing problem, Jonsson says, “but at the same time, we learn a lot from it. And this is what science is about.”
Researchers haven’t independently verified, let alone had time to fully understand, the AI-produced proofs, which both firms have published on GitHub in both natural language and its machine-checkable Lean format. OpenAI has asked the UC Santa Barbara computer scientists who originally proposed the hypothesis, plus an MIT academic who has refuted a version of ETH, to rally researchers to unpack the proofs. So far, this effort includes a Google form asking for volunteers and feedback, and a commitment from OpenAI to fund a conference on the topic.
UC Santa Barbara professor Daniel Lokshtanov plans to join the effort, as he estimates the result—if confirmed—will render him “galactically wrong” and make around 50 of his published papers either “pointless” or in need of a revisit.
“It’s just a giant bomb dropped into the middle of the field,” he says. “It’s really cool and terrible at the same time.”
Thore Husfeldt, head of the algorithms research group at the IT University of Copenhagen, had spent most of this year thinking about one single problem in his subfield. “As far as I can tell, it’s now all irrelevant,” he tells WIRED. Having first formulated a version of the hypothesis now disproved by OpenAI, he has been writing calculations on his blackboard to figure out what other parts of his work might have become obsolete due to the “once-in-a-generation result.” Unlike the ennui that has gripped math researchers who have faced similarly field-upending proofs generated by AI models, though, Husfeldt expressed enthusiasm about the new results.
The finding is “fantastic,” he says. “Being a mathematician is a lot like stumbling about in a completely dark room,” he explains. “It's like somebody just illuminated an entire subfield in floodlights of knowledge, and now we just run around like overexcited bunnies and look at all the nooks and crannies that we can suddenly explore. So it’s a super exciting time.”
For centuries, science has advanced through making hypotheses and proving them wrong. It also isn’t unusual for an academic to be scooped or have their work otherwise undercut by another research group. But AI has accelerated this, obliterating whole research programs and spooking researchers in specific fields of math and science who wonder where they stand now that machines can outperform them.
“The last few months have been really tough. It's a lot of doom and gloom, because every week, or every second week, the results announced by AI just annihilate the ongoing research projects of many people,” Husfeldt says. “That is psychologically taxing for many people,” he says, adding that his department has considered hiring an occupational psychologist because “some people are really depressed and really sad.”
Researchers have also been overwhelmed by the volume of content now being produced, thanks to AI, including slop-level results. Midway through the interview, Husfeldt receives what he suspects to be an AI-generated 17-page paper on the consequences of the ETH result from a random Gmail account. He won’t read it: “Reading math is a very big investment of cognitive time,” he says.
OpenAI has directly contributed to this; earlier this month, it dumped 722 manuscripts on 400 problems on GitHub, to the annoyance of academics , who complain this makes it difficult to digest the results. Adding to the frustration were several documents that contained errors, reflecting what some mathematicians saw as a hasty rollout designed to juice the company’s planned initial public offering rather than moving the field forward. This time around, OpenAI’s 60-odd-page paper on ETH seems to be written better than the companies’ past publications, academics tell WIRED.
They are now scrambling to unpack the paper and find what other results they can quickly deduce from it.
If ETH is false and it doesn’t, in fact, take exponentially more time to solve problems as they become more complex, that’s “exciting,” says Victor Lagerkvist, an associate professor at Linköping. He plans to return to problems he had previously given up on under the assumption ETH was accurate.
OpenAI’s finding could also have impacts on the cryptography that underpins web security, which is based on the assumption that certain mathematical problems take an impractically long time to solve. While this particular result doesn’t directly affect cryptography, “it should definitely scare some cryptosystem designers,” says Lokshtanov.
That’s why continued human and AI-assisted work in theoretical computer science is important, Husfeldt adds: “We want the open scientific process to identify our misunderstandings about computation, in particular because lots of modern digital infrastructure is built on assumptions about computation.”
As for Linköping’s Jonsson, he plans to revisit both his own and others’ papers that hinge on ETH being true, and believes his conference paper may eventually be salvageable through another method. He’s excited to look into the details of OpenAI’s proof and see what he can learn from it and apply it to new problems. Even though it undoes the assumptions underpinning his work, having a verdict for ETH is something he could only “dream of” before, he says. “These are exciting times,” he adds. “Most people would never experience anything like this in their career.”
“I don’t care if it's a human-written proof, or it's written by AI, or if an alien transmitted this proof to us. If it’s true, then we must simply use it in the future.’’

articles.title_orig: Villa Vie Odyssey passenger says warning signs were there long before Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Villa Vie Odyssey passenger says warning signs were there long before Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
A US cruise ship MV. Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville southern Cambodia, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
A couple passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, stands for an interview with his wife, Lynn Motoya, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
A sibling passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Carol Larson, 69, left, stands for an interview with her sister, Crystal Lavering, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over."
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, late Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

articles.content_orig:
Iran's Intelligence Ministry said Thursday that it had dismantled four alleged terrorist cells and arrested 16 suspects in the central and southern parts of Sistan and Baluchestan Province, while detaining three more individuals accused of gathering and transmitting information about security and defense sites in the country's southeast.
In a statement, the provincial intelligence directorate said the operations were carried out in recent days following public tips and ongoing intelligence and operational surveillance, in cooperation with other provincial security forces. It alleged that the cells were affiliated with terrorist groups linked to the United States and Israel.
The ministry said some of the 16 detainees had arrived from abroad. It also alleged that several were involved in the killing of law enforcement personnel in Iranshahr. The suspects have been handed over to judicial authorities, according to the statement, carried by Iran's official IRNA news agency.
Security forces reportedly seized a cache of weapons and ammunition, including nine Kalashnikov rifles, two American-made M4 rifles and seven handguns.
In a separate operation, authorities arrested three people accused of collecting and transmitting information on the locations of military headquarters and defense and security facilities in southern Sistan and Baluchestan to networks the ministry described as linked to U.S. and Israeli intelligence and media operations.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said Thursday that its electronic warfare unit had intercepted and safely landed a U.S. reconnaissance drone west of the Strait of Hormuz, claiming the craft had been conducting surveillance of Iranian air defense systems along the Persian Gulf coastline and the strait.
"Through an offensive electronic warfare operation, the fighters of the IRGC Navy's electronic warfare unit, with the help of Almighty God, successfully managed to safely land an American terrorist army reconnaissance and deception drone of the MQM-170 type in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, after detecting and identifying it and taking control of its guidance and control systems," a statement from the IRGC navy read.
The bulletin added that the IRGC had "determined that the aircraft had taken off from the coast of one of the countries on the southern shores of the Persian Gulf."
Vice President JD Vance has sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei seeking to restart peace negotiations, according to multiple reports, but President Trump insists it is a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he is still mulling whether to resume major military operations against Iran or make a peace deal after next week's midterm elections, according to various outlets.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Vance was engaging directly with Mohsen Rezaei, one of Iran's most powerful hard-liners, in an effort to revive negotiations, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter.
Vance sent the letter to Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' longest-serving former commander, at President Trump's direction, according to The Journal. The initiative seeks to establish whether Washington and Tehran can find common ground to avert a renewed conflict, the paper reported.
According to The New York Times , the letter, sent last week via Qatari mediators and delivered to Rezaei on Sunday, proposed an early meeting between American and Iranian officials, with Vance offering to lead the U.S. negotiating team.
The Times said Rezaei was expected to issue a formal response by Thursday. The letter did not specify a date or location for negotiations, but U.S. and Iranian officials were quoted by the newspaper as saying direct talks could begin as soon as next week in Qatar or Turkey.
According to Axios , Vance's letter explicitly stated that any negotiations aimed at preventing new U.S. military strikes would require discussions on Iran's nuclear program.
Asked Wednesday about Vance's contact with Iranian officials, Mr. Trump told reporters he had not sought to renew peace talks, but "what that is, they [Iran] need help with medical supplies and various things. He [Vance] asked me what I thought and I said, 'If you want to do that that's okay.' Basically it's getting supplies in to help people who are not well."
An official briefed on the diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war.
A response is expected from Tehran by the end of the week, most likely Saturday, the official added.
On Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , Reuters reported.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' said Thursday that three oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines while attempting to transit what it described as "the unauthorized southern route" through the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy's public relations office said the incidents occurred over the past 24 hours, adding that the vessels were subsequently stranded along the southern shores of the strait.
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a southern shipping lane through the vital waterway, which President Trump himself declared mine-free at the end of August. Iran insists vessels can only transit the strait through routes it administers closer to its coast in the north of the strait, in coordination with Iranian authorities.
"These oil tankers had switched off all their radar and navigation systems," the IRGC added, referring to a common practice for vessels trying to avoid either U.S. or Iranian-imposed blockades in the strait and surrounding waters.
The vessels, "disregarding warnings from the IRGC Navy, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized southern route of the Strait of Hormuz when they struck naval mines and exploded," the IRGC said.
The IRGC said it held the vessels' owners and crews responsible for using the route that Tehran has warned against for months.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a Pentagon official has told CBS News, after he was accused of leaking classified information related to the Iran war.
Sylvia was removed on Wednesday as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, becoming the latest in a series of generals to be ousted by Hegseth.
U.S. officials have told several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections – as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter told the Associated Press.
President Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, stressed. He has, however, repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections are over.
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation have put the region on alert for a possible return to major operations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by Mr. Trump, but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.

articles.title_orig: Christine Lagarde to Step Down as Chief of European Central Bank
articles.title_zh: Christine Lagarde to Step Down as Chief of European Central Bank
articles.content_orig:
Departure of Lagarde, seen as candidate to take over World Economic Forum, comes as eurozone struggles with weak growth and inflation
Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, is stepping down nine months early, ending months of speculation about her future.
The European Central Bank (ECB) announced on Thursday morning that Lagarde would step down as its president on 7 February 2027. Her term was scheduled to run until the end of October next year.
The ECB’s governing council thanked Lagarde warmly and gave her a longstanding ovation, as it met to set interest rates across the eurozone.
In a video message on social media, Lagarde said it had been a “great pride and huge privilege” to serve at the ECB. “I think that I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future,” she added.
Lagarde has been seen as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab, stepped down last year after being accused of financial and ethical misconduct, which he denies.
Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is struggling with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.
The European Council appoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone.
Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank, said: “The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027.
“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Élysée Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”
Lagarde joined the ECB in late 2019, shortly before the start of the Covid pandemic . During her tenure the ECB has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war and the Middle East conflict and Donald Trump’s trade war.
after newsletter promotion
The ECB is widely expected to keep interest rates on hold on Thursday afternoon.
Lagarde was wearing two plasters on her face in her video message, which she said was because of “a small surgery earlier in the week”. She added: “Follow doctors’ orders and get your skin checked regularly.”

articles.title_orig: European Union backtracks on Canada becoming ‘associate member’
articles.title_zh: European Union backtracks on Canada becoming ‘associate member’
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has dropped the idea that Canada should become an “associate member” of the bloc, according to media reports.
In a joint draft Canada-EU statement, the terms “associate member” and “associated membership” have been removed, the German news agency dpa and the Reuters news agency reported on Thursday, adding that officials planned to make the statement public on Friday.
The reports come as the EU-Canada summit in Montreal, hosted by Canadian Prime Minister ⁠Mark Carney, is expected to start later on Thursday.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen raised the prospect of Canada becoming the 27-nation EU’s first “associate member” , a striking overture as both seek to pivot away from the United States under President Donald Trump.
However, Reuters and dpa report that von der Leyen’s suggestion of associate membership has been a divisive issue in negotiations among EU countries over ⁠the summit declaration, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and several other leaders of fellow member nations pushing for the terms to be removed from the draft, citing diplomats.
The statement now calls for an “ever closer association” between Canada and the EU, and includes a joint initiative to improve international connectivity between Europe, Canada and Asia through “new ⁠subsea cable infrastructure”.
It also proposes conducting a joint feasibility study on Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and ⁠enabling young Canadians and Europeans to work across the Atlantic.
Deeper ties to Europe are an important part of Carney’s strategy to reduce Canada’s economic and security reliance on the US since Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods. Still, Canada’s efforts to draw closer to the EU risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the US continue.
Trump previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable” and said if he interpreted the move as a “hostile act”, the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.
Carney has aimed to deepen ties with the EU, Canada’s second-largest trading partner, since trade relations with the US, Ottawa’s largest economic partner, have been hampered under Trump.
The Canadian leader told reporters on Tuesday that the summit would be the launch of formal negotiations between the EU and Canada that would take another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”

articles.title_orig: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.title_zh: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.content_orig:
Students gifted only water celery or white wormwood, choosing these fragrant plants to symbolise a pure pursuit of knowledge
While it is common for Chinese people to hold banquets for teachers upon graduation as a way of honouring them – a traditional value – in ancient China, students expressed their respect for teachers differently: by presenting them with vegetables.
The tradition began in the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC). On the first day of school, students wore blue gowns and brought their teachers wild vegetables they had gathered themselves. They then bowed reverently before memorial tablets honouring ancient sages. The ceremony was followed by a group dance, which also expressed the students’ respect for their teachers and their dedication to their studies.
Not just any vegetables could be presented to teachers on this day. Water celery and white wormwood were preferred because they were seen as clean, fragrant and ethereal, symbolising the students’ pure pursuit of knowledge.

articles.title_orig: Alphabet and Microsoft are on both sides of the AI boom's biggest bills: Chart of the Day
articles.title_zh: Alphabet and Microsoft are on both sides of the AI boom's biggest bills: Chart of the Day
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street bought Microsoft and sold Alphabet after the two reported quarterly earnings Wednesday night. Both rent computing power to the AI labs and own stakes in them, but this quarter Microsoft cashed in while Alphabet's bets cost it.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) stock rose about 2% after hours, while Alphabet ( GOOGL , GOOG ) fell over 9%, on track for its worst day since October 2023, after its sales came up short .
For Microsoft, the labs show up as sales. OpenAI paid it $10 billion in the quarter that ended in September, according to Microsoft's quarterly filing. That's about 11% of Microsoft's $92 billion in revenue, and more than its Xbox and Windows businesses brought in combined.
Some of that money is still owed. OpenAI's unpaid bills to Microsoft rose to about $7 billion from $6 billion three months earlier. Microsoft also owns about 24% of the ChatGPT maker, but the stake barely moved its profit this time.
The order book cooled, too. Microsoft's backlog — revenue customers have signed up for, but Microsoft hasn't yet booked — slipped to about $677 billion, and new bookings fell 12% from a year earlier. CFO Amy Hood blamed "large Azure commitments in the prior year" for the tough comparison.
Alphabet's bets on the labs worked the other way. Its stakes in other companies, including roughly 14% of Anthropic and a piece of SpaceX ( SPCX ), supplied about $6 of its $9.11 in per-share profit in the second quarter.
This time they cost it. A nearly $9 billion loss on those holdings cut earnings by $0.55 a share, to $2.12. CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the call that the loss came "primarily" from SpaceX, whose stock dropped about 12% during the quarter.
Alphabet is also footing the bill to build. It spent $51 billion on data centers and equipment in the quarter, more than double a year earlier, and burned about $9 billion in free cash flow — the cash left after those investments — for a second straight quarter. Microsoft generated about $19 billion and said it expects to stay positive this fiscal year.
To cover the gap, Alphabet bought back no stock, sold about $29 billion of bonds and $12 billion of new shares, and nearly tripled its long-term debt this year to about $125 billion. Meta ( META ) took a similar route with its nearly $100 billion stock sale .
The payoff is showing up in Google Cloud, where revenue doubled to about $31 billion and the backlog of signed contracts rose to $561 billion from $514 billion three months earlier. Anthropic has committed at least $115 billion to Google for computing power, according to its IPO filing, about a fifth of that backlog by Yahoo Finance calculations.
The next swing could come from Anthropic itself. Its IPO could start trading as soon as Nov. 16 , and once it does, Alphabet's stake gets valued at the market price each quarter. At the reported $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation, that could turn the drag back into a windfall by year-end.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella doesn't want to lean on the labs forever. Asked on the call where Azure's AI growth is coming from, he said he's after breadth, not "four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you and you can show a few quarters of growth."
"That's not a business as far as I'm concerned," he said.

articles.title_orig: How Netanyahu Used Fear, Again, to Win More Votes Than Anyone Else
articles.title_zh: How Netanyahu Used Fear, Again, to Win More Votes Than Anyone Else
articles.content_orig:
Israeli flags hang at a shop as a bicyclist carrying children passes by, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, in Tel Aviv, Israel, the day after Israel's general election. David Goldman/AP hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — With 90% of the votes counted on Thursday, Israel's election has reached a deadlock — there is no clear winner, with neither side securing a majority in parliament.
The remaining votes to be counted are not expected to change the outcome, paving the way for weeks of negotiations to form a coalition government and for a prime minister to be chosen. Netanyahu's Likud party and his allies have so far won 53 seats and Eisenkot's political bloc has secured 48 seats in parliament.
The winning party needs a coalition of 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Israeli parliament, or Knesset, in order to form a government. The final results will depend on the math and negotiations among broader alliances.
Arab-led parties, representing Arab voters who make up about 20% of Israel's population, have gained about 19 seats, a historic showing in the Knesset. The socially conservative United Arab List, or Ra'am, and the left-wing Joint List could be kingmakers. But Arab leaders have been demonized in Israel.
Netanyahu's far right coalition has refused to partner with them. Before the election, Eisenkot ruled out bringing Arab parties into his government. But he has also left open some room for collaboration, with a set of conditions, including for parties to denounce "Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be destroyed".
On Wednesday, Netanyahu's Likud party claimed the elections were "stolen" by Arab parties, saying it was providing evidence to the police. Critics viewed the allegation as an attempt to prevent the opposition from partnering with Arab parties to unseat him.
According to election officials, Israeli voter turnout on Tuesday was at more than 77%, the highest in more than two decades. Tens of thousands of expatriates flew in from abroad to cast their ballots in the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack and the war in Gaza.
Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister, with almost two decades in office across multiple tenures, but Israelis are divided over his leadership.
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar ("Straight") party, waves an Israeli flag onstage following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election in Tel Aviv, Israel, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Ariel Schalit/AP hide caption
Many question Netanyahu's ability to keep them safe after the Hamas attack, the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. Nearly 1,200 people were killed when Hamas attacked army bases, residential communities and an outdoor music rave — and 251 people were taken hostage back to Gaza.
Israelis have been reeling from reports that the government had received repeated warnings from countries in the region that Hamas was planning a major assault on Israel.
What happened in return was an Israeli military onslaught that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, and left most of Gaza destroyed. Today, Israel is fighting back against charges of genocide while Netanyahu faces an international arrest warrant for alleged war crimes.
Israel's wars in Gaza and the region, and its policies in the occupied West Bank, have badly strained its relations with many international governments. Public support for Israel in the United States has plummeted, worrying many Israeli voters.
Still, many other Israelis are fed up with the world's rebuke over the Gaza war and more than 67 percent of Israelis in a July 2025 poll said they were not very troubled about the suffering of people in Gaza. Netanyahu's supporters have said the wars he has led across the region, from Gaza to Lebanon to Iran, have restored Israel's security.
At Netanyahu's election night party on Tuesday in Jerusalem, giant screens played Hollywood-style videos of soldiers marching, airstrikes blowing up buildings and other destruction. Some clips appeared to show massive explosions of villages in Lebanon, where Israeli destruction of civilian infrastructure has drawn condemnation from human rights groups as potential war crimes, which Netanyahu's government denies.
A post shared by NPR (@npr)
The videos also repeatedly showed President Trump shaking hands with and endorsing Netanyahu . The two leaders have discussed plans to potentially launch major attacks against Iran , which could take place after U.S. midterm elections. Trump urged Israeli voters to reelect Netanyahu to "finish the job that we started."
Supporters of his Likud party at the event struck a defiant tone. When asked if Israel went too far in the war in Gaza, 24-year-old Ori Hazan replied: "We will keep fighting them, and this is now the ideology, this is the policy. You fight us, we will kill you, OK? That's it."
Israeli analyst Danny Citrinowitz told NPR Eisenkot would likely face increased pressure to join Netanyahu in a unity government especially if Netanyahu decides to join the U.S. to resume the war on Iran.
"Netanyahu definitely has an incentive to go to war, he understands that returning to war against Iran while forming a government will serve his interest," said Citrinowitz, who used to head the Iran desk in Israeli military intelligence.
NPR reported last week that the U.S. and Israel could be preparing for a possible attack as early as next week after US midterm elections.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu waves to supporters at Likud party headquarters in Jerusalem following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election, Wednesday. David Goldman/AP hide caption
With the race so close, election officials told NPR they expect to finish counting votes — including hundreds of thousands of ballots from Israeli soldiers — by Thursday afternoon.
President Isaac Herzog said he expects to be handed the official election results next week. Then he will "begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every faction, asking questions, and holding discussions," he said.
Whichever candidate comes out on top is expected to get the first chance to try to form a governing coalition. The party will have six weeks to do that. Both blocs are expected to engage in horse-trading to try to form a government. This has always been the case as no party in Israel's parliamentary system has ever won outright.
Israeli settlers line up to vote at a school serving as a polling station during Israel's general election in the settlement of Kiryat Arba, in the occupied West Bank, Tuesday. Leo Correa/AP hide caption
Herzog said he hopes there won't have to be an election do-over if the process breaks down.
"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind," he said.
Eisenkot's Yashar party includes figures from Israel's political center and moderate right. The opposition parties he would partner with range from the right and center to the liberal left. He has pledged not to join a government led by Netanyahu.
Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party, which is part of Eisenkot's bloc, called on X for the bloc to form a coalition with the Arab parties.
"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't stop with the racism," he said. Even though it would help the Eisenkot bloc win, since the 2023 attack on Israel there's been heightened mistrust of Arab political leaders.
Another possible scenario is if neither side is able to form a government, leaving Netanyahu as a caretaker prime minister, with a repeat election held next year.

articles.title_orig: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.title_zh: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
While Alphabet's ( GOOGL ) stock is getting crushed on Thursday after earnings, Microsoft ( MSFT ) is getting a pass.
Another way of saying it: Microsoft shares aren't trading down in sympathy.
And there is one simple reason why this is the case.
Microsoft's quarter is being seen as one of higher-than-expected growth that is sustainable, while Alphabet's quarter was sluggish and hinted at slowing growth rates in coming quarters.
Microsoft's Azure sales growth came in about 300 basis points above analyst estimates. Overall sales for the important cloud business grew 48%, excluding currency fluctuations.
Execs guided to 49% to 50% Azure sales growth in the current quarter, ahead of consensus estimates by four percentage points.
The company's capex came in about $5 billion below estimates, and other parts of the business showed sales upside.
Sales and earnings for the quarter came in ahead of analyst forecasts.
"Net/net, these results increase our confidence in the company's ability to sustain mid/upper-teens revenue growth and that strong cost of goods sold/expense operational efficiencies should be supportive of expanding operating margins," said stifel analyst Brad Reback.
Microsoft shares rose 4% in pre-market trading.
Alphabet shares tanked 10% in pre-market trading after a third quarter that could best be characterized as a letdown, both on its own and versus Microsoft.
First, Google's search business notched sales of $63.4 billion, below the $64.9 billion expected. The miss fueled fears Google's search empire is being chipped away by the likes of Claude and ChatGPT, despite massive investment by Google.
Second, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion. In a market getting jittery about negative free cash flow at Big Tech (see the reaction to Meta's ( META ) results last week, when it also had negative free cash flow for the first time in years), Google's print stunk up the joint.
"Alphabet's 3Q results reinforced concerns we had heading into the print, re: Search is decelerating and margins have peaked near-term. This could create an air pocket over the next 1-2 quarters as investors await signs for whether this is transitory or structural," KeyBanc analyst Justin Patterson said.

articles.title_orig: Xbox Mythic achievements now live for all console players
articles.title_zh: Xbox Mythic achievements now live for all console players
articles.content_orig:
The official public October 2026 update for Xbox consoles has begun rolling out this evening (October 28th), featuring a whole bunch of new features highlighted by the long-awaited arrival of Mythic Achievements .
As per the update notes on the Xbox website , there are 10 new features that are arriving via the October update, many of which have been in testing with Xbox Insiders in recent weeks, such as the ability to choose a startup animation .
There are also a bunch of bug fixes in the update, which are as follows:
If you want to download the update immediately, you can do so by going to "Settings", "System" and then "Updates", and you should find it waiting for you in there. Alternatively, you can wait for the update to automatically install to your system in the coming hours.
Here's a list of those 10 new features, along with details on each of them:
Whether you've spent years chasing every achievement, or are simply proud of the games you've finished, Mythic Achievements recognise some of the biggest accomplishments in your XBOX history. You earn a Mythic Achievement when you complete all original achievements for a game. Achievements added later through DLC or updates aren't required, and once you've earned Mythic status, it's yours to keep.
Viewing disc to digital licences you no longer have access to will now open a console native experience instead of a web page. Find this in Settings > General > Personalisation > Games & apps.
You can now view, sort, and delete local game saves that aren't currently in use, helping you make space for the games you're currently playing. Whether you want to delete a single large save file or clear all unused local saves at once, you now have more visibility and control over your console's storage.
You can now choose which animation you see when starting up your console, with options spanning from XBOX One through the latest generation. This new setting can be found under Settings > System > Startup. The existing setting that lets you choose to play the startup animation without sound has also been moved to this page.
You can now enjoy higher-quality remote play streaming to your XBOX Series X|S console, with support for up to 1440p resolution and increased video bitrates for sharper visuals and smoother gameplay on supported devices.
This release contains significant changes to underlying party chat infrastructure designed to enhance the future reliability and security of parties.
We've heard from players who want more control over what shows up in the recent games and apps list at the top of Home. You can now remove any item in that list using the Menu button, including the Play History tile, making it easier to keep Home focused on what matters most to you. You can also enter a new immersive background mode that lets your dynamic or custom background take centre stage. Simply press the Right thumbstick button on your controller from anywhere on Home to fade away the UI and enjoy your background without distractions.
A new local search feature to quickly find specific games and achievements within large lists available in My games & apps, official club achievement lists, and the gaming tab in your profile. Local search works alongside existing filters and sorting options to help you find what you're looking for more quickly.
Games that you play via XBOX Cloud Gaming will now be automatically added to the Games section of My games & apps. To remove these, use the Menu button.When network conditions allow, downloads will now continue in the background while you stream, helping reduce wait times and keep gameplay uninterrupted.
Now you can view detailed information for every badge displayed on a profile, including high-resolution artwork and details about when and how it was unlocked. Whether you're revisiting your own collection or exploring another player's profile, it's easier than ever to discover the story behind each badge and celebrate the achievements, milestones, and experiences they represent.
Liking anything here in particular? Tell us down in the comments section below.
Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

articles.title_orig: An ‘Endless’ Cruise Around the World Is Suspended, Leaving Passengers Stranded
articles.title_zh: An ‘Endless’ Cruise Around the World Is Suspended, Leaving Passengers Stranded
articles.content_orig:
A US cruise ship MV. Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville southern Cambodia, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
A couple passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, stands for an interview with his wife, Lynn Motoya, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
A sibling passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Carol Larson, 69, left, stands for an interview with her sister, Crystal Lavering, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over."
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, late Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX stock slides back toward $140 as smaller space names leave it behind
articles.title_zh: SpaceX stock slides back toward $140 as smaller space names leave it behind
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SpaceX took its worst one-day hit last Thursday since early August, when its biggest share unlock yet freed up to 1.3 billion shares to trade. Roughly a week later, it's back at the same floor, and the rest of the space trade has left it behind.
SpaceX ( SPCX ) shares slipped again on Thursday during premarket trading, along with nearly every space stock.
$140 has been SpaceX's floor since the summer. It marked the top of the stock's August trading range before a breakout, and it sits about halfway between the August low near $108 and the $172 ceiling that capped rallies in June and October.
That makes $140 support , a price where buyers have repeatedly stepped in. They did it twice this month, and the stock is back there again.
SpaceX fell about 9% on Oct. 22 as those shares unlocked.
Since then, the smaller names have done the running. Rocket Lab ( RKLB ), Firefly Aerospace ( FLY ), Intuitive Machines ( LUNR ) and AST SpaceMobile ( ASTS ) gained roughly 8% to 14% from the Oct. 22 close through Tuesday, while SpaceX barely budged.
That bounce followed a much rougher month for the group: over the past 30 days, those four are down roughly 20% to 35%, compared with a loss of about 3% for SpaceX.
The pullback comes as investors gear up for Anthropic's IPO, the next mega-listing, with JPMorgan again set to lead retail share sales as it did for SpaceX. SpaceX sits about a third below its June record close near $212.
A sustained break below $140 would open the door to a deeper slide toward the August low near $108. To turn the chart around, bulls first need to get back above the 50-day moving average, near $150, before taking another run at $172.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) report after the bell. How much more they plan to spend building AI data centers is the number most likely to move a stock that's now mostly an AI company .
